title: Arrokoth, the snowman at the edge
hook: The farthest world ever visited is two flat lumps gently stuck together.
peek: On New Year's Day 2019, NASA's New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, more than 6 billion km from the Sun. It turned out to be two flattened lumps that touched at walking pace, almost unchanged since the Solar System formed.
lede: After flying past Pluto in 2015, NASA's New Horizons spacecraft headed deeper into the Kuiper Belt, a ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune. On 1 January 2019 it passed a small object about 36 km long. The first pictures showed a shape like a reddish snowman. It is still the most distant world any spacecraft has visited up close.

bullets.text: Arrokoth was only discovered in 2014, when astronomers searched with the Hubble Space Telescope for something New Horizons could reach after Pluto. Before the flyby it was a faint dot of light.
Later images taken as the craft sped away showed the two lobes are not round balls. The larger one is flattened like a pancake, and the smaller is shaped more like a dented walnut.

The neck between the lobes shows no sign of a violent crash. The two pieces probably orbited each other and drifted together at walking speed or slower, a clue that such bodies formed gently from clouds of pebbles.
Its early nickname was Ultima Thule. In 2019 it was renamed Arrokoth, a word for sky in the Powhatan language, with consent from Powhatan elders.
